title: Lobster Trap: OpenClaw in Containers from Local to K8s and Back — Sally Ann O'Malley, Red Hat

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling

domains.label: Developer Platforms
domains.rationale: The talk focuses on containerizing, deploying, and scaling AI agents across Podman, Kubernetes, and OpenShift as a developer platform substrate. The infrastructure targets software builders using containers and Kubernetes to run and manage agent workloads. Coverage spans local deployment via Podman, Kubernetes scaling, and ongoing operations including backup, recovery, and observability. Requires working knowledge of containers, Kubernetes, and CLI tooling but is presented accessibly with live demonstrations. Conference talk with live demonstrations of the OpenClaw installer, provider selection, and agent management.

summary: Sally Ann O'Malley, a Red Hat engineer of 10 years, spent her first seven years working on containers, Linux security, and Kubernetes in OpenShift before transitioning to an emerging tech role and then to AI-focused work about three years ago. She discovered OpenClaw during a staycation, found it on GitHub with an MIT license, and immediately began containerizing it for OpenShift. When colleagues warned that OpenClaw was a security nightmare, she countered that Red Hat's core competency is running applications securely, framing this as a golden opportunity. She advocates running everything in containers for reproducibility, secret isolation, portability across infrastructure, volume-backed backup and recovery, and natural sandboxing. She introduces her personal forever claw named Shubra with two sub-agents: Joy for astrology readings and Bruno for daily Bruins hockey briefings. For secrets, she uses Podman's secret feature to store API keys on the host, mounted into the container as references. OpenClaw adds a second indirection layer with its own secret refs, creating a pointer-to-ref-to-outside-secret chain that prevents API keys from appearing in logs. The installer also works with Docker, converting envars into OpenClaw secret refs. She shares an Nvidia case study: approximately 10 engineers each run their own OpenClaw in Kubernetes for model evaluations, with one engineer doing work that previously required six. Her workplace standardization vision involves a curated baseline OpenClaw for new hires containing company-approved MCP servers, authentication, team-specific skills, and integrations, which fans out across the team. The demo shows the local installer spinning up an agent named Joe in approximately two seconds, with provider selection (OpenRouter/Gemma primary, Anthropic fallback, local endpoint option), an optional OpenTelemetry collector with Jaeger for observability, and an SSH sandbox feature for running commands in a remote workspace. She demonstrates switching between agent instances (Joe and Larry, the latter with an MCP server and sub-agent configured through the form), then transitions to Kubernetes connected to a kind cluster, showing an agent named Carl running in Kubernetes and another accessible in OpenShift. She mentions a Docker colleague named Eric who created InferRS, a project that runs Gemma very fast using Turbo Quant.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and background
sections.summary: Sally introduces her 10-year tenure at Red Hat: first 7 years on containers, Linux security, and Kubernetes in OpenShift, then moved to emerging tech org, then 3 years ago transitioned to AI work involving lots of Python and markdown.

sections.title: Discovering OpenClaw and security pushback
sections.summary: Sally found OpenClaw on GitHub during a staycation, noted its MIT license, and immediately built the image and ran it locally and on OpenShift. Colleagues warned it was a security nightmare, but she argued that running applications securely is exactly what Red Hat does.

sections.title: Benefits of containers and Forever Claw introduction
sections.summary: Containers offer reproducibility, secret isolation, portability across infra, volume-backed backup/recovery, and natural sandboxing. Sally introduces her forever claw Shubra with two sub-agents: Joy (astrology) and Bruno (Bruins daily briefings). She backs up her forever claw nightly.

sections.title: Agent directories, tools, and secrets management
sections.summary: Agent directories with tools, skills, and MCP servers can be mounted into containers for instant startup. Podman secrets store API keys on the host, mounted as refs into containers. OpenClaw adds a second layer with its own secret refs. Kubernetes secrets work similarly for distributed deployments.

sections.title: Scaling with Kubernetes and Nvidia case study
sections.summary: Sally envisions agents running everywhere and communicating. For business use cases, Kubernetes provides security and scale. An Nvidia team of 10 engineers each runs OpenClaw in Kubernetes for model evals, with one engineer doing the work of six. AI enables focusing on creative rather than tedious work.

sections.title: Backup, recovery, and workplace standardization vision
sections.summary: Volumes (Podman) and PVCs (Kubernetes) provide clean backup/recovery for agent state. Sally's vision: new hires receive a curated baseline OpenClaw with company-approved MCP servers, authentication, team skills, and integrations, fanned out across teams then personalized individually.

sections.title: Local demo: running OpenClaw with Podman
sections.summary: Demo begins with npm run dev local installer. Sally notes a macOS limitation: containers run in a VM so spawning a container from a container is tricky, while Linux can do this natively. She begins spinning up a pod named Joe with opinionated options and default port 89.

sections.title: Demo: secrets, providers, SSH sandbox, and Podman launch
sections.summary: Sally bumps the port to 99 and shows Podman secret mappings for API keys already on her system. The installer also works with Docker by converting envars to OpenClaw secret refs. She selects OpenRouter with Gemma as primary provider and Anthropic as fallback, mentions local endpoint and OpenTelemetry/Jaeger observability options, and demonstrates the SSH sandbox feature that runs commands in a remote workspace using SSH keys and known hosts.

sections.title: Demo: agent status, model switching, and Kubernetes transition
sections.summary: Sally shows the Podman command for launching Joe, checks agent status and models, and demonstrates switching between instances Joe and Larry (Larry configured with an MCP server and sub-agent via the form). She then transitions to Kubernetes connected to a kind cluster, showing agent Carl, and notes OpenShift instances are accessible when connected to OpenShift. She mentions a Docker colleague Eric who created InferRS for fast Gemma inference with Turbo Quant, and closes by encouraging the audience to try running OpenClaw containers.
